stories.summary: Rwanda Eyes Nuclear Tech to Improve Agriculture 16 September 2026 The New Times (Kigali) By Alice Umutesi The governement is exploring the use of nuclear and isotopic techniques to improve agricultural productivity, food safety and resilience to climate change, Minister of State for Infrastructure Armand Zingiro has said. ALSO READ: Inside Rwanda's nuclear development ambitions Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines "In agriculture and food security, Rwanda recognises the significant potential of nuclear and isotopic techniques to improve agricultural productivity, food safety, nutrition and climate resilience," said Zingiro, who led the Rwandan delegation attending the conference. Nuclear technology is used in agriculture primarily through radiation and isotope techniques to improve crop yields, control pests, manage natural resources, and ensure food safety. "Rwanda has therefore expressed its interest in participating in the Atoms4Food initiative, jointly supported by the IAEA and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations." The initiative supports countries in using nuclear and other technologies to improve agricultural and livestock productivity, manage natural resources, reduce food losses, improve food safety and nutrition, and strengthen resilience to climate change. Zingiro said Rwanda plans to work with the IAEA and FAO to assess its national priorities and capacities and develop a programme tailored to the country's needs.

stories.title: US announces South Africa visa curbs over race claims
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5MgVL US President Donald Trump clashed with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office in May 2025 Image: Jim Watson/AFP Advertisement The United States has announced a new visa restriction policy for South Africans amid continuing claims that the white, Afrikaner minority in the African country is suffering from "race-based discrimination." US President Donald Trump 's administration has ⁠criticized South Africa over a range of issues including land and employment laws that are meant to redress inequalities that Black people still face 30 years after the end of apartheid . "As President Trump has made clear, the South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed. "The United States will not allow such behavior to go unchecked," Rubio said. "These actions directly undermine peace, economic stability, and the rule of law, and they are incompatible with the pillars of America's foreign policy." The US ambassador ‌to South ⁠Africa ⁠said ​​on ​social media ‌on Wednesday that ‌the visa restrictions were "only the first ⁠step ​in ​a ​series of ‌escalatory measures." Rubio did not name any individuals to be immediately affected by the restrictions but said they would target those who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa." South Africa: Discrimination claims based on misinformation South African President Cyril Ramaphosa says there is no evidence of discrimination against white people in his country and has called for global efforts to debunk ⁠false ​stories about white persecution. Nevertheless, the Trump administration has continued to attack South Africa. In 2025, Trump berated President Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a "white genocide" in South Africa. He has also hit the country with high tariffs, boycotted a G20 summit in Johannesburg and launched a special program allowing thousands of white Afrikaners to settle in the United States. stories.title: Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5MeN4 Women make up less than a third of lawmakers in the US Congress Image: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement The Global Gender Gap Report 2026, published by the World Economic Forum (WEF) on Wednesday, reveals that gender parity worldwide is closer than ever — standing at 69.2%. However, the Geneva-based nonprofit warned that full parity may still be 120 years away and that the progress made so far remains "fragile." The report, which looked at gender parity across workforce participation, education, health and politics in 145 economies, found that women now occupy senior leadership positions in government and business at levels that were rare globally when the index began in 2006. Yet, while women's presence at the top of politics has grown since the first report, the past decade has seen that trend reverse. The percentage of countries led by women peaked in 2022 and has now fallen back to 2016 levels.

stories.summary: Algeria: Threats to Resume Executions After 30 Years Severe Blow to Human Rights VOA Algeria on the map. 15 September 2026 Amnesty International (London) Algeria's authorities must immediately abandon any plans to expand the scope of the death penalty or resume executions after more than three decades without carrying one out, said Amnesty International as the government examines amendments to the penal code that would broaden the use of the death penalty. The organization calls on Algeria's authorities to immediately establish an official moratorium as a first step towards fully abolishing the death penalty. It also urges the authorities to adopt a human-rights centred response to the recent devastating wildfires, including by ensuring effective investigations into all factors that led to the tragic loss of life and accountability without resort to the death penalty. On 30 August, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune instructed the Minister of Justice to amend the Penal Code by 15 September to "reintroduce" the death penalty for intentionally starting or instigating fires. He stressed that anyone sentenced to death would face execution as soon as they have exhausted their right of appeal.

stories.title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade
stories.summary: Illustrations by Diana Ejaita The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls. The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards. The Register of British Slave Traders , a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includes biographical data on every known investor in Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries. It reveals how wealthy individuals , often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.

stories.title: The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans: Britain’s monarchy and the slave trade
stories.summary: A close-up of a King Charles’s eyes beneath a jewelled crown, with silhouetted figures and ships collaged above Composite: Guardian/Diana Ejaita View image in fullscreen A close-up of a King Charles’s eyes beneath a jewelled crown, with silhouetted figures and ships collaged above Composite: Guardian/Diana Ejaita The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans: Britain’s monarchy and the slave trade From Elizabeth I’s backing of early voyages to royal investment in trafficking companies, generations of monarchs were central to Britain’s slave trade Enslaved African people were seared with hot metal brands bearing the royal crown, according to research by historians who have documented the monarchy’s centuries-long involvement in Britain’s slave trade. The Register of British Slave Traders identifies thousands of people who invested in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved Africans, including kings and queens. In response to the Guardian’s reporting of the new research relating to the monarchy, a spokesperson for King Charles said he was “grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed”. Dr Nicholas Radburn, a historian at Lancaster University, discovered evidence of the branding in the archives of the South Sea Company, a British crown-backed enterprise that trafficked thousands of enslaved African people to plantations in the 1700s. Radburn found a letter sent by the company’s board to its agents in Buenos Aires, instructing them to brand enslaved people with hot metal.

stories.title: Monarchs, MPs and merchants: the register laying bare Britain’s slave-trading past
stories.summary: The register builds the most comprehensive single picture so far of those who perpetrated the enslavement of African people. Illustration: Diana Ejaita/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The register builds the most comprehensive single picture so far of those who perpetrated the enslavement of African people. Illustration: Diana Ejaita/The Guardian Monarchs, MPs and merchants: the register laying bare Britain’s slave-trading past Exclusive: New research identifies thousands who profited from trafficking enslaved Africans and traces some financial links to institutions still operating today The big picture The Register of British Slave Traders and the president of Ghana, John Dramani Mahama The enormous scale of Britain’s centuries-long trafficking of enslaved African people, supported by parliament and the monarchy, has been laid bare by new research. The Register of British Slave Traders , the product of a three-year project by a team of specialist historians, documents the investors in Britain’s near 250-year transatlantic slave trade from the first traffickers in the 1560s to abolition in 1807. The register provides biographical detail for as many of 10,500 investors as possible from historical records, building the most comprehensive single picture so far of those who perpetrated the enslavement of African people.

During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses. "Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home. "The threats are manyâ¦ even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten." President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials. During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans. Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country. "We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food.
